vignette:
Michael is forty-five years old, a widower, and a man who has spent his entire adult life learning how to hold still while the world burns around him. He sits in the chair across from me with his hands resting flat on his thighs, palms down, as if he is bracing for an impact that hasn’t come yet. He is a military medic by trade, or rather, he was. He has been on medical leave for the past eleven months, and he is not sure if he will ever go back.

The thing that broke him was not a battlefield. It was a river.

In the spring of last year, Michael was deployed as part of a humanitarian aid operation during catastrophic flooding in a mountainous region of Eastern Europe. His unit was tasked with evacuating civilians from a village that had been cut off by mudslides. He had done this kind of work before—triage in the field, extraction under fire, the grim calculus of who gets lifted first. He tells me he was good at it. He tells me he never hesitated.

On the third day of the operation, the helicopter he was in went down. Not shot down—the pilot lost visibility in a wall of rain and clipped a power line. They crashed into a hillside that was already sliding apart. Michael was thrown clear, but he landed in the floodplain, pinned against a collapsed bridge by the current. He spent four hours in the water. He watched people drown. He watched a mother hand him her baby over the railing of a sinking roof, and then watched her get pulled under before he could reach her. He held the baby against his chest while he clung to a piece of rebar, and he kept holding it even after it stopped moving.

He was rescued by a civilian boat crew. The baby was already gone. He knew that. He knew it in the water. But he did not let go.

Michael tells me this story in a flat, procedural voice, like he is reading from a report he has written a hundred times. He does not cry. He does not look away. But his hands, still on his thighs, are trembling.

Since the crash, Michael has not slept more than two hours at a stretch. He wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced he is still in the water. He can feel the cold. He can hear the sound of the mother’s voice, calling a name he never learned. He has tried to drink himself to sleep, but it only makes the nightmares more vivid. He has tried to stay awake for days at a time, but eventually his body gives out, and he wakes up on the floor of his apartment, disoriented and terrified.

He cannot tolerate the sound of running water. He cannot shower. He washes himself with wet wipes and a basin, and he does it quickly, with the bathroom door open. He cannot stand the smell of wet earth. He avoids the weather forecast. He has not left his apartment in three weeks, except to buy canned food and whiskey at a 24-hour convenience store two blocks away, always after midnight, when the streets are empty.

He tells me he is not afraid of dying. He says that honestly, without bravado. He says he has made peace with that. What he cannot tolerate is the feeling of being helpless. He cannot tolerate the memory of holding that child and knowing, with absolute certainty, that he could not save her. He was a medic. He was trained to act. And in that moment, all his training meant nothing.

His wife died six years ago. Cancer. He tells me that he used to think that was the worst thing that would ever happen to him. He is not sure anymore. He is not sure he knows how to live in a world where he failed the one thing he was put here to do.

He says, "I used to believe that if I just kept moving, I could outrun it. But the water is always there. It doesn't matter how fast I go. It's already inside me."
